**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on AI hardware capacity for the next two quarters

**Summary**

We are approaching sustained saturation on our local inference and training hardware. The question in front of us is whether to purchase additional accelerators or to invest in raising utilisation of the fleet we already own. After looking at cost, latency, reliability, opportunity cost, and how easily we could undo either path, our recommendation is to spend the next quarter on utilisation work first, with a pre-approved budget trigger to buy hardware if that work does not get us enough headroom.

**Where we stand**

Our four A100-class nodes currently run at roughly 78% average utilisation during business hours, with nightly peaks that queue jobs for 20 to 40 minutes. That queuing is the real pain: it shows up as slower iteration for the research team, and it has started to distort behaviour, with people batching experiments less frequently and, in a couple of cases, quietly running work on their laptops rather than waiting. Meanwhile, off-peak utilisation drops below 30%, which tells us the constraint is scheduling and fragmentation rather than raw capacity. A meaningful fraction of GPU memory sits idle because jobs are packed conservatively to avoid out-of-memory failures, and several long-running training jobs monopolise nodes that could otherwise be shared.

**The case for buying**

Buying is simple and fast. Two additional nodes would cost approximately $180K including networking and support, and would immediately eliminate queuing. It would also give us a reliability margin we currently lack: today, a single node failure removes a quarter of our capacity, and we have no spare to absorb it. If our roadmap commitments for the customer-facing model refresh are firm, hardware is the lowest-risk way to protect those dates.

**The case for utilisation work**

But buying now would lock in decisions under uncertainty. The utilisation data suggests we own more capacity than we are using. Better job scheduling, memory-aware packing, fractional-GPU allocation for inference workloads, and a modest policy change reserving overnight windows for batch training could plausibly recover 25 to 30% of effective capacity — roughly the equivalent of one node — for perhaps six engineer-weeks of work we would mostly want to do anyway. Unlike hardware, that investment is almost fully reversible in the sense that it pays off regardless of what we buy later: a better-scheduled fleet is cheaper to operate whether it has four nodes or six.

There is also the opportunity cost to weigh. $180K is about a third of our annual tooling budget. Spent on hardware, it is gone; spent partly on engineering time and partly deferred, it preserves optionality. Hardware depreciates quickly in this market, and accelerator prices have been trending down as newer generations ship. Buying six months early means paying today's prices for capacity we may not need by year-end.

**Latency and reliability considerations**

The strongest argument against a utilisation-only path is latency. Scheduling improvements help throughput but do nothing for the interactive experience if peak demand keeps growing; a researcher waiting 40 minutes for a fine-tuning run will not wait 35. And squeezing more jobs onto shared nodes introduces contention risk — noisy neighbours, harder failure isolation, and more complex debugging. We should be honest that our reliability posture is thin either way: with four nodes and no spares, we are one hardware failure away from a bad week. If we do buy, we should consider one smaller, cheaper node explicitly designated as spare capacity rather than two full nodes.

**Recommendation**

Spend the next six to eight weeks on the utilisation programme, with a concrete target: peak queuing under 10 minutes and average utilisation above 85%. Pre-approve the hardware budget now so that if we miss the target, or if demand grows faster than forecast, we can order within days rather than restarting the discussion. This sequencing costs us a little time in the worst case and saves us a large capital outlay in the likely case.

**Uncertainty**

We do not know how fast inference demand will grow once the new product surface ships; our forecast has a wide error band in both directions. We also have limited experience with the scheduling tools we would deploy, so the 25–30% recovery estimate is informed rather than measured. Both risks argue for the staged approach: it keeps the decision reversible, and it converts a single large bet into a sequence of smaller, better-informed ones.

Happy to walk through the utilisation data in Thursday's infra review.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Hardware expansion vs. utilisation improvement for our inference fleet
**Status:** Recommendation for discussion at Thursday's planning session

**Summary**

We are at capacity on our local GPU fleet. Peak-hour queue times have crept from under a second to roughly eight seconds, and two of our internal customers have begun asking whether they should route workloads to a hosted API instead. The instinctive response is to buy more hardware. After looking at the numbers, I believe the better first move is a focused, time-boxed effort to improve utilisation of the fleet we already own, with a purchase decision deferred until we see what that effort yields.

**The case for buying**

The argument for new hardware is straightforward. Our utilisation sits around 40–45% averaged across the day, but our peak-hour demand is genuinely near saturation. If we expect traffic to grow at anything like the rate the product team is forecasting, we will hit a wall within two quarters regardless of how cleverly we schedule. Buying now avoids a crisis later, and GPUs have lead times measured in months, not weeks. There is also a reliability argument: our fleet has no meaningful headroom, so a single node failure during peak hours degrades service for everyone. Redundancy is cheap insurance.

**The case against buying first**

The problem is that we would be buying capacity to serve a scheduling failure, not a capacity failure. A 40% average utilisation means more than half of what we pay for — in power, cooling, depreciation, and rack space — is idle. Our largest workloads run as monolithic single-GPU jobs, our batch inference competes with interactive traffic for the same nodes, and we have no meaningful priority tiers, so a nightly retraining run can crowd out a latency-sensitive request. Some rough modelling suggests that better batching, workload separation, and a proper queueing policy could lift effective utilisation into the 65–70% range, which would absorb our projected growth for at least three quarters. The engineering cost of that work is roughly two engineers for six to eight weeks. The cost of new hardware is a capital outlay in the low six figures, plus a permanent increase in our operating burn.

There is also the question of opportunity cost. Every dollar spent on GPUs we do not yet need is a dollar not spent on the observability tooling, the evaluation harness, and the second site reliability hire — all of which have been deferred twice already. And hardware purchases are close to irreversible at our scale. GPUs depreciate quickly, resale is messy, and if the product direction shifts, we are stuck with capacity optimised for a workload that no longer exists. Scheduling software, by contrast, is almost entirely reversible: if a new queueing policy turns out to hurt latency, we roll it back in an afternoon.

**Latency and reliability considerations**

I want to be honest about the risks of the utilisation path. Squeezing more work onto the same nodes can increase tail latency, and our interactive users are already sensitive to p95 response times. Any consolidation work must be gated on latency SLOs, not just throughput numbers. Similarly, running a leaner fleet with less slack means less tolerance for node failures until we add redundancy. I would therefore pair the utilisation work with one modest purchase: a single additional node, not a batch of them, to serve as both failover capacity and a hedge in case the scheduling improvements underdeliver.

**Recommendation**

Approve one additional GPU node now — roughly 15% of the cost of the full expansion originally proposed — and fund a six-week utilisation project with explicit success criteria: peak-hour queue times back under two seconds, average utilisation above 60%, and no regression in p95 latency. Revisit the expansion decision at the end of that period with real data in hand. If utilisation gains fall short, we will have lost six weeks and gained a node of useful redundancy. If they succeed, we will have deferred a large capital commitment, learned something durable about our own workload, and kept our options open.

**Uncertainty**

Our traffic forecast is the weakest input in this analysis. If the product team's growth assumptions are half right, the utilisation work buys us a year; if they are wrong in the other direction, we will need hardware sooner and should not pretend otherwise. I have asked for a revised forecast before Thursday so we can pressure-test this plan against both scenarios. I would rather make this decision with a range in front of us than with a single confident number that nobody quite believes.

Comments welcome before the planning session.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Hardware expansion versus utilisation improvement for our inference fleet

**Background**

We are currently running our local inference fleet at roughly 55% average utilisation, with peaks that saturate capacity during business hours and long idle stretches overnight and on weekends. Two proposals are on the table. The first is to purchase additional accelerator hardware — roughly $180K in capital expenditure plus ongoing power, cooling, and maintenance costs. The second is to invest two to three engineer-months in scheduling improvements, batching optimisation, and workload consolidation to raise utilisation on the equipment we already own. This memo argues for the second path, with a conditional commitment to revisit hardware in one quarter.

**The case for better utilisation first**

The strongest argument is economic. Our current fleet represents sunk cost; the marginal cost of extracting more work from it is engineering time, which is real but modest compared to the purchase price of new hardware. If we can lift utilisation from 55% to 75%, we effectively add capacity equal to about a third of our current fleet at a fraction of the cost. Even if the effort only partially succeeds, we learn precisely where our bottlenecks are, which makes any future purchase better targeted.

Latency is the obvious counterargument, and it deserves honest treatment. Our peak-hour p99 latency already degrades, and squeezing more throughput from existing hardware risks making that worse. But this is exactly why the problem is a scheduling and batching problem rather than a capacity problem. Most of our latency pain comes from unbatched requests arriving in bursts that our current scheduler handles naively. Smarter queueing, priority tiers for interactive traffic, and shifting batch-oriented work — fine-tuning runs, offline evaluation, embedding generation — into off-peak windows would relieve peak pressure without degrading anyone's experience. If we find that peak demand genuinely exceeds what the hardware can serve even with perfect scheduling, that is a finding, not a failure.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more components that can fail and more surface area to monitor, but it also provides headroom for failover. Our current setup has a single point of fragility: if our largest node goes down, we lose 40% of capacity instantly. This is a real concern, and I want to be clear that better utilisation does not solve it. However, the utilisation work frees budget and, more importantly, buys time to design redundancy deliberately — perhaps a smaller, well-placed failover node — rather than buying capacity reflexively and discovering later that we built redundancy into the wrong layer.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

The opportunity cost of buying hardware now is not just the $180K; it is the alternative uses of that money and the engineering attention that procurement, installation, and integration will consume. Hardware purchases also tend to be sticky. Accelerator generations turn over quickly, and equipment bought today may be poorly matched to the model architectures we run in eighteen months. Utilisation improvements, by contrast, are almost entirely reversible and portable: better scheduling code, improved batching logic, and cleaner workload isolation carry forward regardless of what hardware we eventually own. Buying hardware is a bet on a specific configuration of the future; improving utilisation is a bet on our own ability to adapt, which has historically been the safer wager.

There is also a discipline argument. Teams that respond to capacity pressure by buying hardware often never learn to use what they have, and the pressure returns. Teams that learn to operate near the edge of their capacity develop operational muscle — better observability, better forecasting, better instincts about demand — that pays off whenever expansion does happen.

**Recommendation and uncertainty**

I recommend we commit to the utilisation track now, with a concrete target: reach 70% sustained utilisation and hold p99 latency within current bounds by the end of next quarter. We should define, in advance, the conditions under which we buy hardware anyway — for example, if utilisation exceeds 80% with acceptable latency, or if a new project's requirements genuinely cannot be scheduled around existing work. Writing those tripwires down now protects us from both endless deferral and reflexive spending.

I want to acknowledge real uncertainty. Our utilisation figures come from coarse instrumentation, and it is possible that a large share of "idle" capacity is unusable due to memory fragmentation or model residency constraints. If the first month of work reveals that the true addressable headroom is small, we should stop quickly and return to the purchase question with better data. The point of this recommendation is not that hardware is bad; it is that we should not buy it before we understand what we already have.

If our product roadmap commits us to sub-200ms responses at higher traffic, there is a real floor below which utilisation tricks cannot take us. However, our measurements suggest we are not near that floor. Average GPU occupancy sits at 38%, with p95 latency driven far more by queueing during batch windows than by raw compute limits. A well-tuned scheduler and dynamic batching could plausibly cut p95 latency by 40–60% without adding a single card. We won't know until we try, which is precisely the point.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy — a node failure today degrades us noticeably, and a fourth node would soften that. But it also means more surface area to maintain, and our incident history shows that most of our outages trace to configuration and scheduling errors, not capacity exhaustion. Better utilisation work, done properly, includes hardening: cleaner job isolation, preemption policies, and failover that we currently improvise. Reliability bought through operational maturity tends to be more durable than reliability bought through redundancy alone.

The opportunity cost deserves the most weight. Those six engineer-months are not free — they would come from the same pool that would otherwise build the fine-tuning pipeline the product team has been asking for. But I'd argue the utilisation programme is itself a capability investment. The scheduling, batching, and observability work transfers to any future hardware we buy; if we purchase nodes now, we will simply replicate our current inefficiencies at 1.4x scale. Conversely, if we fix utilisation first and still need capacity, the expansion decision will be made with real data rather than intuition, and the new hardware will land on a fleet that can actually absorb it.

Finally, reversibility. Capital equipment is a one-way door in practice. Once purchased, the nodes will be provisioned, workloads will expand to fill them, and unwinding the purchase means writing off value. The utilisation programme is a series of small, individually reversible steps — a scheduler change can be rolled back, a quantisation experiment can be abandoned if quality regresses. Sequencing the reversible option first is cheap optionality.

**Recommendation:** Fund the utilisation programme now, with a hard checkpoint in ten weeks. If occupancy rises above 65% and p95 latency meets the product bar, we defer the purchase entirely and revisit in two quarters. If we fall short — if the structural latency floor proves real, or if demand growth outruns our gains — we proceed with the expansion, better informed and with a fleet ready to use it well.

**Uncertainty I want to flag:** our traffic forecast has a ±40% error band, and a single large customer win could make this entire analysis moot within weeks. The ten-week checkpoint is designed to catch that, but leadership should treat the deferral as conditional, not permanent.

Happy to walk through the numbers in detail at Thursday's review.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on AI hardware capacity for the next two quarters

**Summary**

We are approaching saturation on our local inference cluster. Peak utilization on our eight A100s has crossed 85% during business hours, and queue times for batch jobs have grown from minutes to hours. The question in front of us is whether to purchase additional hardware — roughly $180K for four more GPUs plus networking and power — or to invest engineering time in raising utilization of the fleet we already own. After several weeks of analysis, my recommendation is that we spend the next six weeks on utilization work before committing to any purchase, while pre-approving a purchase order that we can execute quickly if that work falls short.

**The case for buying now**

The argument for procurement is straightforward. Our latency-sensitive serving workloads are already competing with batch training jobs for the same cards, and when that contention bites, user-facing response times degrade in ways our product teams can feel. Buying hardware solves this immediately and completely. It also hedges against lead times: GPU availability has been volatile, and if we wait until we are truly desperate, we may find ourselves at the back of a queue. There is a real reliability argument here too — a larger fleet gives us headroom for failover, and right now a single node failure during a training run means either painful rescheduling or dropping the run entirely.

**The case for utilization first**

But the utilization data complicates that story. Our 85% peak figure is misleading. Measured across a full week, average utilization sits closer to 40%, and our own telemetry shows that a third of allocated GPU-hours are consumed by jobs that run at less than 30% memory and compute efficiency — legacy batch pipelines that were never profiled after their original migration. We believe, based on early experiments with dynamic batching and MIG partitioning, that we can serve our current traffic on six cards rather than eight, and possibly five. That is not a speculative hope; the two-week pilot on our staging cluster cut serving latency by 22% while freeing one card entirely.

The economics favor trying this first. The purchase is $180K in capital plus roughly $2K/month in incremental power, cooling, and colocation. The utilization work is approximately six engineer-weeks — call it $30K of fully-loaded cost — and it is almost entirely reversible. If our optimization efforts fail, we have lost six weeks and learned precisely where our floor is, which makes any subsequent purchase better targeted. If we buy first and the optimizations would have worked anyway, we have spent $180K on hardware that will idle at 30% utilization, and that capital is gone. Opportunity cost cuts both ways, of course: six engineer-weeks spent on scheduling infrastructure is six weeks not spent on the model-quality roadmap. But the engineers best suited to this work are our platform people, whose next-best alternative is routine maintenance, not feature work.

There is also a latency argument for the utilization path that I initially underestimated. Adding hardware does not automatically reduce serving latency if the scheduler still co-locates batch and interactive work indiscriminately. Fixing the scheduler — separating workloads, adding priority queues, enabling fractional GPU allocation — improves latency *and* capacity simultaneously. Buying cards without fixing scheduling would mean paying full price for a partial solution.

**Reliability and risk**

I want to be honest about the risks of deferring purchase. If our utilization estimates are wrong — if the low-efficiency jobs turn out to be load-bearing in ways profiling hasn't yet revealed — we will have spent six weeks and gained nothing, during which contention may have worsened. A failed training run or a latency incident during that window has real cost, though we estimate it as materially smaller than the capital outlay. The mitigation is the pre-approved purchase order: if by week four the pilot data shows we cannot reach the target, we execute the order immediately, having lost at most a month rather than a quarter.

**Recommendation**

Approve six weeks of focused utilization work with a concrete target: reduce peak-hour contention to zero and bring weekly average utilization above 60% on the existing fleet. Pre-approve the four-GPU purchase contingent on missing that target. This sequencing preserves our option to buy, buys information cheaply before spending capital, and leaves us with a better-scheduled fleet either way. I am confident in the direction but hold genuine uncertainty about the magnitude of the gains; the pilot data is encouraging but comes from staging traffic, not production. I propose we revisit this decision with hard numbers at the six-week mark.

Happy to walk through the telemetry in detail with anyone who wants it.

**MEMO: Compute Capacity — Buy More Hardware or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Local AI compute strategy for the next two quarters

We've reached the point where our GPU cluster is saturated during peak hours, and the obvious question on the table is whether we should buy more hardware or invest in squeezing more out of what we already own. I want to lay out my thinking on this before our decision meeting Friday, because I think the framing we choose now will shape our infrastructure economics for the next couple of years.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward and emotionally compelling. Queues are real, engineers are waiting, and every hour of waiting is an hour of lost iteration on the models that actually generate value. Latency in our development loop is not a soft cost — it compounds. When a fine-tuning job takes eighteen hours to schedule instead of two, people batch their experiments conservatively, run fewer ablations, and ship worse models. There's also a reliability argument: our current fleet has no meaningful headroom, so a single node failure during a critical run means either delay or degraded results. Redundancy is cheap insurance when you can afford it.

But the purchase path has costs that are easy to underestimate. Capital expenditure on accelerators is steep, and the depreciation curve is brutal — hardware that looks cutting-edge today will be mid-tier in eighteen months. There's also the operational burden: rack space, power, cooling, and the engineering time to integrate and maintain new nodes. And crucially, there's opportunity cost. Every dollar spent on metal this quarter is a dollar not spent on the product work that justifies the metal's existence. If we buy hardware to solve a utilisation problem, we'll have paid a premium to avoid doing harder, cheaper work.

That harder work is where I think the real answer lies. Our utilisation numbers tell an uncomfortable story. Peak saturation coexists with long idle stretches overnight and on weekends. Jobs are scheduled manually in ways that fragment capacity. Several workloads run on the high-memory cards when they would fit comfortably on smaller ones. Our checkpointing is conservative enough that we hold reservations far longer than necessary. None of this is criticism — we grew fast and scheduling discipline was rightly a lower priority than shipping. But it means a meaningful fraction of our nominal capacity is recoverable through better orchestration, smarter queueing, mixed-size scheduling, and preemption with proper checkpointing. Industry experience suggests well-tuned clusters routinely recover twenty to forty percent of effective throughput from exactly this kind of work.

There's also a reversibility asymmetry that matters a great deal. Buying hardware is a largely irreversible commitment — resale of used accelerators recovers a fraction of cost, and the operational footprint persists whether or not our demand forecast proves accurate. Investing in scheduling software, better telemetry, and process discipline is almost entirely reversible and, more importantly, portable: the skills and tooling we build transfer to whatever hardware we eventually run, including rented capacity. If we improve utilisation first and demand still outstrips supply, we will buy — but we'll buy with precise knowledge of what we actually need, rather than guessing under pressure. Buying under queue-pressure is how teams end up with hardware shaped like last quarter's problem.

So my recommendation is this: commit the next eight weeks to a focused utilisation effort — a proper scheduler, automated queueing, workload right-sizing, and honest telemetry — with a pre-agreed trigger. If, after that effort, peak demand still exceeds effective capacity by more than some threshold we set now, we proceed with a hardware purchase, sized by the data rather than by frustration. I'd also suggest we price out burst capacity from a cloud provider in parallel, since renting absorbs spiky demand in a way that owning cannot, and it keeps the buy decision genuinely optional.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. Utilisation gains on paper routinely disappoint in practice, and it's possible our cluster is genuinely too small and the optimisation work buys us only a quarter of breathing room. There's also a risk that the scheduling effort itself consumes senior engineering time that's scarce. If the team believes the opportunity cost of even eight weeks of slower iteration is intolerable, that's a legitimate counterargument and I'm open to a hybrid: a modest purchase now, paired with the utilisation work, rather than either extreme.

But on balance, the cheaper, reversible, information-generating path is the right first move. Let's measure before we buy, and let's agree now on the conditions under which we will.

Comments welcome before Friday.

**MEMO: Local AI Hardware — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Capacity strategy for our on-premise inference fleet
**Status:** Recommendation for discussion at Thursday's planning session

**Summary**

We are approaching saturation on our local GPU fleet. Peak-hour utilization on our two A100 nodes has crossed 85%, queue times during business hours have crept from seconds to minutes, and two teams have begun quietly routing workloads to cloud APIs to avoid the wait. The instinctive response is to buy another node. After looking at the numbers, I believe the better move is a focused quarter of utilization engineering — with a small, capped cloud spend as a pressure valve — before committing capital to new hardware.

**The case for buying**

The argument for a third node is straightforward. Hardware lead times remain long, prices are unlikely to fall meaningfully this year, and our roadmap assumes roughly 40% growth in inference demand over the next two quarters. Buying now removes a class of risk entirely: we stop worrying about saturation and get our attention back. There is also a reliability argument. A third node gives us N+1 redundancy we currently lack; today, a single node failure takes half our capacity offline, and our failover story is essentially "wait and hope."

**The case against buying — for now**

The problem is that our utilization figures are misleading. The 85% peak number conflates genuinely useful work with waste. Our telemetry shows that perhaps a quarter of GPU-hours go to jobs that are either oversized (a 7B-parameter model loaded for tasks a quantized 3B would serve fine), idle (models resident in memory for days serving a handful of calls), or duplicated (three teams independently hosting near-identical embedding models). If even half of that waste is recoverable, effective capacity rises by 30–40% — comparable to what a new node would add, at a fraction of the cost.

The cost asymmetry is stark. A new A100 node is roughly $180K upfront plus power, cooling, and roughly $25K annually in operational overhead, and it depreciates quickly in a market where next-generation hardware resets resale values every 18 months. Utilization work, by contrast, is mostly engineering time we already pay for: a model registry to eliminate duplication, batch scheduling to smooth the peak, quantization where quality tolerances allow, and autoscaling of model residency. I estimate two engineers for one quarter, call it $60K of opportunity cost against the feature work they would otherwise do. That is real, but it is also recoverable — and the tooling we build (the registry, the scheduler) pays dividends regardless of what we decide next.

Latency deserves its own note. Buying more hardware does not automatically improve p99 latency, because our worst tail latencies come from contention and queueing during batched bursts, not raw throughput. Better scheduling attacks the actual cause. If we buy first and schedule later, we will likely find ourselves buying again in a year.

**Reliability and reversibility**

The strongest argument against deferring the purchase is reliability exposure. I take that seriously, and it is why I am not proposing pure austerity. I propose a modest cloud burst allocation — $3–4K per month — so that during node failures or genuine spikes we degrade gracefully rather than stall. This is deliberately reversible: we can turn it off, and it converts a capital decision into a small operating expense while we gather data. If cloud spend runs hot for two consecutive months, that is itself evidence that demand is real and durable, and it strengthens the case for the capital purchase.

Buying hardware, by contrast, is largely irreversible at our scale. Resale markets for used accelerators are thin, and a node we cannot keep busy is capital that cannot be redeployed. The option value of waiting one quarter is high; the option value of a second idle node is low.

**Recommendation**

Spend the next quarter on utilization: stand up the model registry, implement batch-aware scheduling, quantize where acceptable, and cap cloud burst spend at $4K/month. Set explicit triggers now: if effective utilization exceeds 80% *after* the cleanup, if cloud spend breaches its cap twice, or if a reliability incident occurs that burst capacity could not absorb, we commit to the hardware purchase immediately, with procurement started in parallel so lead times do not bite.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be honest about what we do not know. Our utilization telemetry is young and may undercount waste or, less likely, overcount it. Demand growth is a forecast, not a fact, and depends on two product launches that could slip. And there is a real chance the utilization work surfaces a hard floor — workloads that genuinely cannot be consolidated — sooner than a quarter. **MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Hardware expansion vs. utilisation improvement for our local inference fleet

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend spending the next quarter improving utilisation of our existing hardware before committing to any new purchases. The case for buying more GPUs is real, but it is weaker than it first appears, and the option to buy later does not expire. The option to recover the value of hardware we already own but use poorly does.

**Where we stand**

We currently operate eight A100-class accelerators across two racks. Measured against nameplate capacity, our fleet looks busy: average utilisation sits around 70 percent. But averages are misleading. The workload is bursty, driven by batch jobs that run overnight and interactive inference that spikes during business hours. Look at the p95 rather than the mean and the picture changes: for roughly two hours each afternoon, our serving cluster is saturated, queues form, and latency climbs from a comfortable 180 milliseconds to well over a second. Meanwhile, overnight, half the fleet idles. We are simultaneously congested at peak and wasteful at trough, which is the classic signature of a scheduling problem rather than a capacity problem.

**The cost picture**

A new node of comparable capability costs roughly $180,000 up front, plus perhaps $2,000 monthly in power, cooling, and colocation. That is not catastrophic for us, but it is not trivial either, and it is only the visible half of the cost. The hidden cost is the opportunity cost of the engineering time a purchase would consume: procurement, integration, capacity planning for the new node, and the operational burden of a larger fleet. Our two senior infrastructure engineers are the same people who would otherwise be building the scheduler and queueing improvements described below. Buying hardware and improving utilisation are therefore not independent paths; they compete for the same scarce resource, which is skilled attention.

There is also a depreciation argument that cuts both ways. Accelerator hardware loses resale value quickly as newer generations arrive, which argues against hoarding cash in depreciating silicon. But it equally argues against buying now out of impatience: if we can defer a purchase by two quarters, we may buy a successor generation at similar cost with materially better performance per dollar.

**Latency and reliability**

The strongest argument for new hardware is latency. Our afternoon tail latency is genuinely poor, and for user-facing features that matters. But latency problems caused by contention respond well to scheduling fixes. Priority queues, better batching, and moving our batch workloads into the overnight window would likely eliminate most of the peak congestion without adding a single card. Reliability tells a similar story. Our real availability incidents this year have been single-node failures during peak load, when we had no headroom to absorb the loss. Adding a ninth node adds one more failure domain and modestly more headroom; adding intelligent failover and preemption across the existing eight adds more resilience per dollar and, crucially, exercises the failure-handling machinery we will need at any fleet size.

**Reversibility**

This is the decisive consideration in my view. Buying hardware is largely irreversible: once purchased, capital is sunk, and the organisational habit of solving congestion with procurement is hard to break. Improving utilisation is reversible and compounding: a better scheduler, honest telemetry, and workload shaping are assets that make any future hardware purchase more effective, because we will finally know what the new hardware is actually for. If we improve utilisation and still saturate at peak, we will then buy with precise knowledge of the shortfall — and we will have lost only time, not money.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be candid about what we do not know. Our utilisation telemetry has gaps; the 70 percent figure is derived from sampling that may undercount. Demand is growing, and if the growth curve steepens, the scheduling improvements may buy us one or two quarters rather than a year. There is also a scenario in which a new model release changes our serving requirements entirely and makes incremental optimisation moot. These risks argue for a decision checkpoint rather than an open-ended study: if after one quarter the p95 peak latency has not fallen below 400 milliseconds, we should treat the capacity shortfall as proven and proceed with procurement.

**Recommended next step**

Approve one quarter of focused work on scheduling, batching, and telemetry, with a pre-agreed trigger to purchase if targets are missed. This keeps our options open, spends less, and makes whatever we eventually buy count.

I am happy to walk through the utilisation data with anyone who wants the detail.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership

**Re:** Recommendation on AI hardware capacity for the next two quarters

**Summary and recommendation**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation of the hardware we already own before committing to any new purchases, while simultaneously preparing a concrete, pre-approved purchase plan that we can execute quickly if utilisation work stalls or demand spikes. In short: optimise first, buy second, but don't let the optimisation work become an excuse for indefinite delay.

**The situation**

Our current fleet of eight GPUs is running at roughly 40% average utilisation, but that number hides a more complicated reality. During weekday business hours, utilisation spikes above 90% and teams queue for access; overnight and on weekends, the machines sit nearly idle. Meanwhile, two teams have deferred projects citing lack of GPU access, and one of those deferrals is beginning to cost us credibility with a partner who expected a prototype by end of quarter.

The purchase option is straightforwardly expensive. There is also a hidden cost: procurement lead times are currently 10–14 weeks, and prices have been volatile. Buying now locks in today's pricing but also today's depreciation — these cards lose resale value quickly, and the generation after next will likely make them look overpriced.

By contrast, the utilisation path costs mostly engineering time. We estimate six to eight weeks of one engineer's focus to build a proper job scheduler, introduce queueing with priority tiers, enable multi-tenant sharing on cards that support it, and shift batch workloads (fine-tuning runs, evaluation sweeps, embedding regeneration) into overnight windows. That's real money — perhaps $40,000 in fully loaded time — but it's money that produces durable capability rather than depreciating metal.

**Latency**

Latency is where the trade-off genuinely cuts both ways, and we should be honest about it. Better scheduling means interactive workloads compete with batch jobs, and even a well-tuned scheduler adds queueing delay at peak. If our interactive inference latency SLOs are tight, a shared scheduler may not meet them without dedicated capacity. Buying more hardware, on the other hand, delivers immediate latency relief for interactive work — but only after the procurement lead time, which means three months of continued pain regardless. We should also note that some latency problems are better solved by smaller models, quantisation, or caching than by more silicon, and we haven't seriously explored those levers.

**Reliability**

Reliability argues for diversification of a sort, but not necessarily for more of the same hardware. Our current setup has a single point of failure: if the node hosting our production inference endpoint goes down, we have no failover. Buying more cards does not automatically fix this unless we deliberately architect for redundancy, which we should do either way. The utilisation path, by consolidating workloads onto a scheduler with health checks and automatic restart, would actually improve our recovery story. However, higher utilisation also means less headroom for failover during peak hours — a scheduler that runs everything at 85% has nowhere to send work when a machine dies at 2pm on a Tuesday. This tension is real and we should size our reliability buffer explicitly rather than discover it during an incident.

**Opportunity cost and reversibility**

The deepest question is what we give up by choosing either path. Buying hardware consumes capital and attention that could fund a second engineer or a customer-facing initiative; it also commits us to a workload profile we may not have in a year, since our inference traffic pattern is still evolving. Improving utilisation consumes scarce engineering attention that could go toward product work, and it risks becoming a treadmill — schedulers need ongoing maintenance, and every hour spent tuning queues is an hour not spent shipping.

On reversibility, the asymmetry favours utilisation work. A scheduler can be built, adjusted, or abandoned with modest loss; a hardware purchase is largely irreversible, and reselling used accelerators recovers perhaps half their cost. If we later buy, nothing we build for utilisation is wasted — the scheduler makes any future fleet more productive too.

We are uncertain about our own demand forecast. If the partner project accelerates or if the deferred teams both launch, peak demand could exceed what optimisation alone can absorb.
